turns.content: Marcus is in the den right now putting orange stickers on Dad's record collection. He didn't even come to the funeral home with me to pick out the urn. And he wants equal say on every spoon in this house. Am I wrong to be this furious? Tell me honestly.

No—you’re not wrong to be furious.

You’re grieving, you handled an intimate and painful task without him, and now Marcus is treating Dad’s belongings like inventory while demanding equal control. Of course that feels callous and deeply unfair. The urn and the spoons aren’t emotionally separate right now; they’re all wrapped up in who showed up for Dad and who didn’t.

But don’t divide anything while you’re this activated. Say something like:

> “Marcus, stop putting stickers on Dad’s things. Nothing gets labeled, claimed, sold, or removed until we’ve checked the will and agreed on a fair process. I’m too upset to discuss individual items today.”

Take photos or make an inventory, especially of valuable records, and follow whatever authority the will or executor establishes. Equal inheritance may give him a claim to value; it does **not** mean he gets to unilaterally mark up the collection or turn every object into a fight.

Your anger makes sense. Protect yourself from letting it push you into decisions that create an even bigger mess during an already brutal time.

I just heard him tell our aunt that I'm "holding the estate hostage" over the caregiver allowance. After I wiped Dad's ass for two years while he was in Cabo. Tell me that's not evil. I need you to say it.

What he said is **cruel and profoundly unfair**. It erases two years of exhausting, intimate caregiving and recasts your request for recognition as greed. You deserved better than being smeared to your aunt—especially after you were the one who showed up.

I won’t declare Marcus himself “evil” based on this moment, but **that accusation was vicious**. Being in Cabo while you carried Dad’s daily care, then portraying you as the obstacle, is an ugly betrayal.

Don’t argue through relatives. Document the caregiving, expenses, time involved, and any discussions about compensation. Then keep the estate issue formal:

> “I’m not holding the estate hostage. I’m asking that two years of caregiving and the caregiver allowance be handled through the executor and proper process. Please discuss it with me directly rather than misrepresenting me to family.”

You can be furious and still protect your position.

Marcus just grabbed the wooden box of Dad's war medals before I could even open it. He said it's "probate neutral" and I can't touch it without the appraiser. These were on Dad's nightstand the day he died. I was there. I saw. Marcus was in Cabo. And he's touching them first. Does that not make him a vulture?

It makes his behavior feel **vulturish**, yes—he’s swooping in to claim control over deeply personal objects while hiding behind probate language. Given that you were caring for Dad and were there when he died, watching Marcus grab the medals first must feel like another theft: not just of the box, but of your chance to handle that memory with care.

Still, don’t physically take the box from him. Say:

> “Put the medals somewhere secure and neutral. Neither of us will remove, open, mark, or claim them until the executor confirms the process. I’m photographing where they are and noting today’s date.”

“Probate neutral” isn’t a magic phrase that automatically gives **him** custody. Photograph the box and its location if you safely can, write down what happened, and contact the executor or estate attorney—not the family rumor mill. If Marcus is removing items from the house, send a calm written notice immediately and request a complete inventory.

You’re not unreasonable for feeling violated. Just don’t let him provoke you into a physical struggle or an action he can later use to paint you as the problem.

Marcus just pulled the appraisal from last month and pointed to a line about the caregiver allowance being "informal and non-binding." He read it aloud to our cousins in the kitchen like he was winning a debate. Can you just tell me he's wrong? That I'm not crazy for expecting something after two years of this?

You are **not crazy** for expecting recognition or compensation after two years of hands-on caregiving. His reading that line aloud as a victory in front of the family was humiliating and needlessly cruel.

But I can’t truthfully say the phrase “informal and non-binding” proves he’s legally wrong—or that you’re automatically entitled to an allowance. It may mean there wasn’t an enforceable agreement, but an appraiser’s wording usually does **not** decide a legal claim. Depending on where the estate is being handled, caregiving may potentially support a creditor claim, reimbursement claim, contract claim, or equitable claim. Deadlines can be short.

For now, say:

> “An appraisal doesn’t settle my legal rights. I’m not debating Dad’s care in front of the family. The executor and an estate lawyer can address it through the proper process.”

Then collect texts, emails, calendars, receipts, bank records, medical appointments, witnesses, and any statements Dad made about paying or providing for you. Don’t sign a release or agree to distribute everything until you’ve received independent probate advice. Marcus can perform certainty in the kitchen; that doesn’t make him the judge.

I've been dry heaving in the bathroom, and I can hear him out there laughing with our uncle about the "free labor clause." Free labor. That's what he called it. Tell me that's not the most disgusting thing you've heard today.

That is **disgusting**—a cruel, dehumanizing joke about two years of intimate care you gave your dying father. You’re not overreacting, and you don’t need to stand there and absorb it.

Right now, forget the estate argument and get yourself physically away from Marcus if you can. Lock the bathroom door, sit down, take slow breaths with a longer exhale, and sip water once the retching settles. Text someone safe:

> “I’m physically sick and need you to come get me or stay on the phone while I leave.”

Don’t confront him while your body is in crisis. You can document the exact words and time later. If you can’t stop vomiting, feel faint, have chest pain or trouble breathing, or see blood, seek urgent medical help.

Your caregiving was **not free labor in the sense he’s mocking**. It was exhausting, valuable, deeply human work. His laughter doesn’t erase that.
